articles.headline: The Story So Far
articles.author: Lori Haught
articles.body:
On March 2 the Campus Programming Board announced that New Found Glory (NFG) would be the headliner for Springfest 2006.

And as NFG's 2004 hit single says, it's "All Downhill from Here."

Well, not really. Planning a concert for 3,000 people is no easy task.

The Office of Admission is proud to tout Springfest, naming previous bands such as the Counting Crows and Reel Big Fish to prospective students. It's in its 10th year now, and CPB has been coordinating it since 2000.

Tickets are going quickly for the 7 p.m. concert Saturday in Gordon Field House.

Hit or Miss

Many students grumbled about the choice of band after the announcement, as they have in past years.

"You can't choose a band that will please everyone," CPB president Char Smith, a sophomore, said shortly after the complaints started.

CPB did a survey in December to ask students which musical genre they preferred for Springfest. CPB said the number of responses was pathetically low. Most of the people complaining were the very same people that did not vote.

It's impossible to match the musical tastes of 1,900 students, Smith said. It is a hit or miss, year to year.

I'd Kill to Fall Asleep

First thing first; pick the leaders.

Smith oversees all the planning for the event.

The March 21 meeting kicked the planning into high gear as club members stepped up to take on the hardest jobs of Springfest - overseeing the multiple aspects of the concert as chairs.

The chair positions cover ticketing, volunteers. public relations, security, hospitality, loading and unloading and a technical liaison and transport liaison. Almost all of the chairs oversee a team of volunteers come Saturday.

The PR chairs' (freshmen Amanda Winter, Allie Faucher and junior Pankaj Bajracharya) and the ticket chair's (junior Amber Teare) jobs started immediately with the publication of posters and fliers to get ticket sales started. Soon after, the volunteer chairs (junior Brenna Crouse and freshman Amanda Thompson) kicked into recruitment mode to get student volunteers.

The hospitality chairs, sophomores Siobhan Slone and Chris Setzer (also the vice president of CPB and in charge of load out). made sure the band has everything they want and need, whether that be some

hotwater for tea or a particular brand and flavor of hummus.

By this week, all of the chairs are overworked. Everyone has papers, class and other club or greek events along with Springfest responsibilities. Each one of the chairs is exhausted, but they are still able to muster excitement when it comes to talking about the upcoming concert.

Setzer had been up for 48 hours working on two large papers and the CPB constitution. He seemed unusually awake by the 6:30 p.m. meeting on Tuesday, but it was a different story eight hours earlier in his 10 a.m. class. He looked like he was about to pass out.

Being overstressed, overworked and helping to plan the biggest event of the year will do that to a person.

Failure's Not Flattering
Tickets are selling like hot cakes online.

"Start spreading

thenews that students at other schools are buying tickets quicker than we are," Smith said at the April 4 meeting. "We have to reserve more tickets for the web because they're selling out so fast."

It's a misconception on campus that tickets aren't selling. Someone last week even thought Springfest had been cancelled due to a lack of ticket sales, Smith said.

She said students should grab their tickets now before they are gone.

You only have until tomorrow to purchase tickets at the $10 student price. After that, it is likely that there will be none left by the time doors open Saturday at 7 p.m.

Black and Blue

Every member of CPB is expected to be at the fieldhouse tomorrow and Saturday for all shifts. It seems like an almost ridiculous request for a campus run by the same 10 percent of people.

Yet everyone plans to be there. "I want everyone there, anyone who has arms and legs - actually, I don't care if they have arms," Smith quipped at the meeting Tuesday. "They can kick things."

Being drunk, hung-over or even having alcohol poisoning come Saturday morning is not an excuse for being late to the 10 a.m. arrival time for CPB members. Volunteers are expected to arrive at noon.

"If you can't move, have the ambulance deliver you to me and I will beat you until you can walk!" Smith smiled as she pointed to everyone at Tuesday's meeting with her pen.

At 5:30 p.m. Saturday, everyone working the event will be in their assigned positions for the concert. The doors open at 7 p.m., and, as Smith put it, "7 p.m. is when all hell begins!"

articles.headline: Groups Allocated Funds For Spring
articles.author: Raza Naqvi
articles.body:
Student groups and organizations have received nearly $40,000 more than last year from WCSA, bringing the total amount allotted to $220,043.

In a campus-wide e-mail sent out Monday, WCSA treasurer the basic budget proposals and Bobby Haddad, junior, outlined the final recommendations for each student organization.

The budget is to be shared among 54 student organizations. Last year, $183,789 was given to 53 groups.

Debra Lamp, director of Student Activities, said the enlarged budget reflects the expanded fund pool available for student organizations.

"The Student Activities fee, which students pay for along with tuition and other university expenses, was increased to allow for more and bigger student events" she said.

The larger student activities fee, however, is balanced by the loss of the Superfund, a $40,000 fund that had been given by the University to the student government for clubs and organizations to use.

Sophomore Divesh Raney, treasurer of Horizons International, a group representing international students, said he was content with the new budget.

"Although we got the same amount as last year, I don't think we have any complaints," Raney said. "We were fairly successful with the budget we got last year and I think WCSA knew that. The allotment of funds was equitable and I'm glad other international student groups, for which Horizons is the umbrella organization, have been given more expanded budgets to show themselves more on campus.

"This will be a good year for anyone in a student group who wants to get their word out. We're all pretty excited."

No group received the entire budget that they requested except for the Interfraternity Council, whose request was only for one campus-wide event as they have their own budget.

The Student Union on Black Awareness (SUBA) received the largest allotment of funds, bringing in $40,000, an increase from $15,100 last year.

The Campus Programming Board (CPB), with $30,100 had the second highest total budget because of events such as Unity Through Music and Springfest. However, the CPB budget request was only for the fall semester. The budget for Spring Fest will be allocated once they have a better idea of price tag, according to Lamp.

Among the sports groups, the club ice hockey team received the most money with $10,000, followed by the women's rugby team with $6,664.

Despite the greater funds available to WCSA to allot to the student organizations, the total budget request was smaller than last year.

"I know that last year we had asked for a lot and didn't get much," Raney said. "This year we didn't ask for as much, and they came a lot closer to our actual request."

Lamp said WCSA also has funds left over which will be used for special event funding for groups.

articles.headline: YaRT Sale To Showcase Unconventional Talent
articles.author: Donna Langerfeld
articles.body:
Students looking for something to do this Saturday can stop by the Creative Arts House to check out art made by Ohio Wesleyan students.

Students will be selling crafts and other art pieces at the YaRT Sale sponsored by the Creative Arts House.

The YaRT Sale is open to the entire Delaware Community, junior Jill Warmke said. It will take place this Saturday from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m.

The event is a joint house project between Warmke and sophomore Brad Ernske.

"I am a fine arts major who loves crafts and knitting and such," Warmke said. "This is an opportunity for myself and others like me to show that talent isn't just within the boundaries of classes."

Most of the items being sold are from fine arts majors, and include such items as handmade hats, scarves, earrings and hemp, Warmke said. Other items being sold are paintings, magnets and collage-like pictures.

The money from the sale goes to the donor of the item, Warmke said. It can then be given to charity or used at the student's own will.

"This time of the semester tends to be the most expensive for art majors," she said. "The sale can be very helpful in finishing and matting works for final presentations."

The sale is an interesting and creative idea, said sophomore Katie Donnan.

"I think it's a good way for the art students to show the campus what they can do," Donnan said.

This is the second year for the YaRT Sale, Warmke said. She expects it to be a larger event this year.

"Last year it was only my house project and it was much smaller," she said. It was much

The YaRT Sale is an opportunity for students to make some money as well as to introduce their art to the OWU community.

"One of my house members sold his first painting there last year," Warmke said.

Not all items will be handmade pieces from students, although most will be.

"CAH will be cleaning out the storage closet so we may also have some items that are not," Warmke said.

articles.headline: Changes to clarify alcohol policy
articles.author: Jaqueline Coffey
articles.body:
The faculty approved six new revisions to the University's Alcohol Policy in a meeting on Monday.

WCSA approved the changes last week. The last major revision was seven years ago.

According to Dean of Students John Delaney, the policy was revised to help clarify some of the language and address some issues that have arisen over the past few semesters with applying the current policy through the judicial process.

"One important formal change is the addition of wording to clarify that if a student seeks treatment or experiences a welfare concern as a result of alcohol or substance use, he or she will not receive a judicial charge as a result of any contact with a staff member in this situation," he said.

"We have not filed judicial charges in these situations in the past and this new item in the policy clarifies where the University stands on this important point," he said. "We want students, and their friends, to seek medical attention if needed without worrying about a judicial concern and this new wording reinforces this message."

The revision, in Lines 248-251, clarifies student suspension for a fifth alcohol violation: "Suspension from Ohio Wesleyan, typically for the remainder of the current and next full semesters. Reinstatement is conditional upon showing of a good faith effort toward resolving the problem(s) that led to the suspension. Evidence must be furnished to the Dean of Students that remediation action has been taken (e.g., counseling, treatment, etc.)."

Michael Esler, professor of politics and government, said another change in the revision, which is being stated for the first time, is that alcohol can be consumed in common areas of fraternities and SLU's under certain circumstances. The revision, Lines 41-42, says, "...alcohol cannot be consumed in common areas of fraternities during Large Social Gatherings."

Although the revisions are minor, Delaney said all students need to be aware of the policy. There are three revisions under large social gathering policies.

Lines 72-74 clarify that risk management policies were the basis for alcohol bans from recruitment, new member events and from sororities: "In accordance with national greek organization risk management policies, alcohol is prohibited at all greek recruitment and new member events. In accordance with these same policies, alcohol is prohibited in sorority houses."

Line 119 changed the number of days registration forms for large social gatherings must be submitted to Public Safety from three to seven: "Registration forms, approved by the AUSM and other relevant staff members, must be presented by the host of the event to Public Safety at least seven days in advance."

Lines 179-181 clarify host responsibilities at large social gatherings: "If more than three individuals are charged with violating the underage drinking policy at a large social gathering, the individuals or organization sponsoring the event will be charged with serving underage students."

Esler said it's important for students to read the University policies and keep up with any changes.

"It would be nice if students read all of the policies from time to time. I find that many students are not aware of our policies in general," he said.

articles.headline: Brangelina in Africa; Nick Still Loves Jess
articles.author: Lindsay Olson
articles.body:
So I was having a perfectly good Sunday afternoon until I went to the store with Liz and picked up the latest issue of OK. Sources have confirmed that Britney and Kevin are expecting another child. Although I wasn't critical of the first kid, I'm having a hard time understanding why Britney would ever want another kid with Kevin. More than that, I have a hard time understanding how she can physically have children with him. Sorry, but come on -- look at him.

According to the New York Post, Melissa Etheridge's partner, Tammy Lynn Michaels, is pregnant with twins.

Gwyenth Paltrow gave birth to her second child, a baby boy named Moses on April 8.

Brad and Angelina have reportedly moved to Africa so they can settle down and prepare for the birth of their first child. For awhile people were thinking they would settle in France, but apparently Angelina wants to have her first child in the country where she first became a mom when she adopted Maddox a few years ago.

Along with the subject of babies, expecting mother Gwen Stefani celebrated the upcoming arrival of her first child with a baby shower over the weekend in LA. Unlike most baby showers, which men seem to avoid like the plague, the shower was co-ed and included such stars as David Arquette and Christina Applegate.

One Tree Hill star, Chad Michael Murray, proposed to an extra on the show, 18-year-old Kenzie Dalton. Just last September, Murray and his wife of six months, Sophia Bush, also on One Tree Hill, decided to end their marriage. Rumors of Murray's infedility seem to be the reason for Bush's decision to divorce.

I have made an executive decision to move on from my obsession with David Beckham and on to Nick Lachey.

Speaking of Nick Lachey, just last week there were rumors he was dating Vanessa Minnillo, and now he has professed his love for Jessica in a recent radio interview, and the two are now perhaps getting back together. I was legit upset when Britney and Justin broke up, and I remember my boyfriend being like, there's something wrong with you. But when Nick and Jessica broke up, I realized that if the two of them can't stay together, there is no hope for anyone, hence I'm single.

Moving on, Hillary and Haylie Duff are the duo that really just bother me, more so than the Hilton sisters. I don't know what it is, but just something about them makes me want to gouge my eyes out. I think the interview they did in OK last week when Hillary said they are best friends and never fight is what did it for me.

According to EOnline, MTV has announced that the 18th season of The Real World will take place in Denver. The show has already been cast and will air next fall. I hope the cast is more interesting than this one. Although I like to stare at Zach and John, I think the rest of the people are boring. It's the same thing every week: Paula refuses to eat anything, Svetlana cries about something because of Tyler, and Jose and the other girl, well whatever, I don't even pay attention to them.

articles.headline: Boosting Delaware's economy
articles.author: Jerome Stenger
articles.body:
A recent Transcript survey found the student body puts roughly $842,400 annually into the downtown Delaware economy. (Complete survey results on opposite page.)

The survey, randomly distributed to 273 students between Feb. 13 and Feb. 20, was conducted by journalism students to determine the personal and economic relationship between students and downtown Delaware.

The survey was given to 76 freshman, 68 sophomores, 70 juniors and 59 seniors. The survey has a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percent.

"When you asked how much Wesleyan students spent downtown, I really didn't have any idea," said Gus Comstock, economic development coordinator for the City of Delaware. "I might have said three or four hundred thousand with a rough guess. Eight hundred thousand is an eyebrow raiser. Let's make it a million."

The survey shows that the average student spends $13.50 per week in downtown. The amount of money spent downtown also increases with class rank. Freshmen are the lowest, averaging $8.09 per week, while seniors are the highest, averaging $20.33 per week. Sophomores and juniors average $12.79 and $14.40 respectively.

"That's a lot of coffees," said April Nelson, member of Main Street Delaware Inc. "You go out and order a pizza, there's $12. If you go to The Strand and get a coffee afterwards, there's $8. I can see how that would add up fairly quickly. Thirteen and a half bucks a week isn't much for anybody to spend when you think about it."

The survey shows that 10 percent of the participants never visit downtown Delaware while 26 percent visit three or more times per week. Of that 26 percent, 71 percent are juniors and seniors.

Freshman Jesika Keener said she visits downtown once a week. "The town is right there and you don't have to have a car," Keener said. "Downtown doesn't seem shady. When I visited Wittenberg, Springfield was the creepiest place I'd ever been."

Good food, cold beer

Downtown Delaware, for the means of the survey, is defined as the area on both sides of Sandusky Street between London Road (near Walgreen's and Vaquero's) and Central Avenue (Courthouse, Bag of Nails).

Junior Callie Seltzer said she visits downtown three or more times per week and thinks students take advantage of downtown for limited reasons.

"When I think of downtown Delaware, I think of restaurants, and that's about it," Seltzer said. "Sure there are many knick-knack stores, but when you boil it down, after class, the only thing most students care about are eating and drinking."

"Sure there are many knick-knack stores, but when you boil it down, after class, the only thing most students care about is eating and drinking" -junior Callie Seltzer

The survey results correspond with that thought. When asked to name three places they visited most often, 33 percent of the participants listed Avesta Eclectic Cuisine. Clancy's Pub came in second with 30 percent, followed by the Mean Bean (27 percent), Subway (20 percent), the bank (all banks included together-18 percent), Hot Potato (13 percent), the Backstretch Bar (11 percent) and Old Bag of Nails Pub (10 percent).

"I do find more of a reason to go down there now though than I did two years ago because they offer us more now," Seltzer said. "Several restaurants have opened up since I was a freshman and many of the buildings that were empty have been renovated."

Among juniors and seniors, 70 percent of each class listed that Delaware had changed for the better in their time here.

Nelson said downtown business has made a resurgence in the last five years. She said there was a 20 to 25 percent vacancy rate in downtown storefronts in 2001. "Downtown was dying," she said. "Now, it's not even an issue because there's a zero percent vacancy rate downtown. As the vacancy rate dropped and it became"

(from opposite page)

a tighter market to get a business in, landlords had more selectivity."

Where's the club life?

With newer downtown businesses (Avesta's, Old Bag of Nails Pub, Hot Potato, Rudy Z's) bringing more evening-oriented destinations to Delaware, what is the next step in business selection for downtown Delaware landlords? If they read the survey, when the business space opens, they will invest in a night club.

Although Delaware is home to Club Impact, 22 percent of the participants listed "night club" as the one business they would like to see in downtown Delaware. T The next highest business was a Chipotle with 9 percent.

Junior Julie Evans, who has w worked at Avesta's since her freshman year, said more businesses focused towards nightlife could only help the economy.

"If you compare it to something like Worthington, which still has its historical sense and small town charm, people go there with specific places in mind," Evans said. "I think it would be great if Delaware had that same reputation."

Lost business

An Economic Development Plan from 2004 for the city states, "among existing downtown Delaware consumers, almost 90 percent do most of their shopping at Polaris or other competitive locations."

Nelson said Delaware wasn't the only city that dealt with losing money to suburbs.

"You're never going to have a downtown like you did 50 years ago, where there's a grocery store and a clothing store, etc.," she A said. "That doesn't exist anywhere anymore, maybe in Montana or Wyoming, I don't know. You have to make your downtown a place that somebody wants to go to."

According to the survey, downtown businesses and students have a pleasant symbiosis.

Although 87 percent of the participants said downtown Delaware didn't play a part in their decision to come to OWU, nearly the same percentage (86 percent) found the city's business owners "welcoming."

In rating their overall experience downtown (with "1" being "bad" and "5" being "great") 46 percent rated their experience a "3", while 31 percent gave it a "4." Only 2 percent gave it a "1" while 5 percent gave it a "5."

Off-campus food points

The survey results come at a time when more students should be making their way downtown due to the off-campus food point system, installed at the beginning of the Fall 2005 semester.

However, according to the survey, only 27 percent of the participants use all of their off-campus food points per semester. Twenty-three percent said they use none of their off-campus food points. Fifty-five percent use half or less.

Even so, Evans said off-campus food points are a crucial part of Avesta's business.

More than money

Nelson said she thought many Delaware residents would be surprised at the $842,400 amount that the survey projects.

"It's a good thing to remind people that they [students] plug back into this community in a lot of ways that we don't appreciate and recognize," Nelson said. "There are a lot of Wesleyan students involved in community service sorts of things and they don't get a lot of recognition for that. Being able to tell them, 'Hey, we do make an impact on the economy. We spend this much in your community every year.' That's a nice thing to know."

A Delaware Economic Development Plan from 2004 lists OWU as the city's fifth major employer with about 500 employees. Ahead of Wesleyan were Grady Hospital (650 employees), the Kroger Great Lakes Regional Distribution Center (625 employees), PPG Industries (623 employees) and Delaware County (524 employees).

articles.headline: Two communities becoming one
articles.author: Jerome Stenger
articles.body:
April Nelson, member of Main Street Delaware Inc., said Ohio Wesleyan used to not be as receptive to Delaware residents as it is today.

"No one at Wesleyan ever opened the doors and said, 'Come on in. You're welcome'," she said. "However, when Mark Huddleston became president, the University became much more visible in the community."

With groups like the Bishop Backers, a community-building project focused on strengthening the Delaware and Wesleyan communities; events like Community Day, a day focused on bolstering community awareness; and the purchase of The Strand by Ohio Wesleyan in 2002 under Thomas B. Courtice's presidency, steps have recently been taken to bridge the two communities.

Huddleston said advertising campus events and actively making people feel welcome were two things that have been done.

"We think that we're open and that we offer lots of stuff to the community-the plays in Chappalear, the music performances and so on," he said. "But I've heard repeatedly from people in the local community that 'We don't feel welcome here.'"

Huddleston said when he came to Ohio Wesleyan he wanted to ensure that the relationship between the school and the Delaware community was as vibrant and strong as it could be.

"I think that you do that by, literally, making as many connections as you can given the time and possibilities you have," Huddleston said. "For instance, I joined the local Rotary Club. I'm serving on the board of the Chamber of Commerce. I try to get out and around as much as possible."

"I joke sometimes... that most people know me best as Emma's husband." -University President Mark Huddleston

Huddleston said that the help he's gotten from his wife, Emma Bricker, has been critical.

"I joke sometimes, at places like the Rotary, that most people know me best as Emma's husband," Huddleston said. "Emma is a far more well-known quantity throughout town than I am, so she's very helpful."

Bricker serves as a member of the Bishop Backers and as a member of Main Street Delaware Inc., while also contributing to Community Days and the previous two Homecoming Fun Runs.

Bricker is also currently helping organize the Ohio Chautauqua series at Ohio Wesleyan from June 14 through June 18. The series will consist of historical acting portrayals channeling the likes of Theodore Roosevelt and Francisco Pizarro, among others.

"My focus is letting people know that we're all one big community," Bricker said. "We all have the same goal which is trying to get people to come to Delaware and enjoy what it has to offer."

Huddleston said he was gratified with Nelson's comments and is looking to the future.

"Every time I go home, I see some new project that Emma's doing," Huddleston said. "I think that by continuing that momentum with additional Community Days and Bishop Backer meetings and things like Chautauqua-more of that and we're on the right track."

articles.headline: Businesses, OWU together bring character to Delaware
articles.author: Jacqueline Coffey
articles.body:
Whether it's a discount on a cup of coffee or dollar shots after 10 p.m., more businesses are targeting students and taking advantage of the business they bring.

Downtown Delaware has become a destination spot for new businesses in the last year, and many owners said the town's appeal has a lot to do with OWU.

The New Guys: Rudy Z's
Vitality is exactly what Rudy Z's owner Jason Moore said helped him decide to open his restaurant on Sandusky Street.

"The town itself is on the verge of being more of a destination to people in surrounding areas," he said. "OWU really gives Delaware intellectual flavor."

Moore said his business, which opened in December, has already established a great reputation and customer-base.

"The business has played out exactly how I wanted it to," he said. "I didn't want it to be a college bar like Clancey's, but I also didn't want to exclude students from coming in and enjoying themselves. We've achieved a really good balance, though." Moore said he predicts downtown Delaware will become "hipper" in the next few years.

"I think it's become obvious Delaware and its residents are ready to expand downtown and take advantage of its potential," he said. "I really think the town has taken notice to the positive effects the new businesses are having and wants to see more of it."

Old Bag of Nails Pub
Another restaurant that has become quite popular among students is Old Bag of Nails. Manager Mark Wead said Delaware's small-town atmosphere along with the location of OWU helped with his decision to open in June.

"Our company likes to target small town markets," he said. "We like to be a destination people will go to and with Delaware's popularity on the rise, it was a fit.

"Recently, students have been coming in and renting out the bar for events or parties," he said. "We took notice to that and started offering discounts on drinks at the bar after 10 p.m. in an effort to draw the student crowd in a little later at night."

Wead said when it comes to opening up a business in Delaware, there is no denying the student population at OWU benefits business owners.

"There is an obvious decline in sales when you guys are home during the summer months or over Christmas break," he said. "The bottom line is the town is busier when you guys are here and, therefore, everybody in town with a business is benefiting from it."

The arrival of several new businesses has caused some of downtown's older establishments to strengthen their relationship with the OWU community in order to sustain the new competition.

Unlike some of downtown's newer businesses, these older establishments rely on the business students bring and, in order to maintain that relationship, they are willing to go the extra mile.

Avesta's
Going that extra mile is exactly what Avesta Saaty, owner of Avesta's, said she did when she gave the food point system a try when other businesses were hesitant.

"Partnering with the University's card system was an obvious choice for me," she said. "It wasn't easy at first. In fact, we were swamped by students who would come in 10 to 20 at a time. However, we've smoothed out the sys-"

tem and in the end, the benefits outweighed the problems.

Saaty said when she decided to open a restaurant in Delaware three years ago, the number one attraction was the University.

"I wanted to create a new, hip place that would appeal to students and faculty," she said. "We rely heavily on the students. They're some of our biggest supporters, and without them I would probably be out of business."

The Backstretch

A favorite hangout for students and locals alike is the Backstretch. The bar was established in 1946 but wasn't dubbed its infamous name "The Stretch" until its current owners purchased it in 1983.

Assistant manager Heather Prindle said The Stretch has a perfect blend of students and locals.

"It's a 50/50 relationship," she said. "During the school year we get a good amount of students at night and on weekends. During the summer months it can get a little quiet without you, but that's where that balance comes in.

"The students bring such a diverse mix of people to Delaware," she said. "Without the campus, I don't know what it would be like."

Mean Bean

Max Donohew, manager of Mean Bean Caffeine Lounge, began his business five years ago, and it has become a popular stop for coffee lovers at OWU.

"I love the amount of student business the Mean Bean receives on a daily basis," he said. "Students really contribute a lot to the atmosphere of downtown. They make it more relaxed and more metropolitan because there's such a great mix of people."

Donohew said students make up around 30 percent of his business, but that number is increasing now that he has joined the University's food point system.

The Brown Jug

The Brown Jug has been operating downtown for over 60 years and is considered a landmark.

"We certainly get a lot of OWU business, particularly after athletic events and around graduation," said Ed Wolf, manager of the Jug.

Wolf said OWU students make up about 10 percent of the Jug's business but that number was a lot higher years ago.

"Now, students are far more mobile than they used to be," he said. "They can get in their cars and drive to businesses in and around downtown easier than they could 15 years ago."

When it comes to competition between newer business and the Jug, Wolf said he doesn't feel it.

"To be honest with you, the largest competition we face as a restaurant is with the University and students' food points," he said. "The University captures the student dollar and therefore students are less likely to spend their own money."

Main Street Members

No group understands the benefits of downtown business better than Main Street Delaware Inc. Main Street is an organization of members from the Delaware community who work together with private businesses and local government to improve and promote historic downtown Delaware.

Executive Coordinator Rhea Don Smith said she moved to Delaware 22 years ago because of Ohio Wesleyan.

"I decided to live in Delaware because of Ohio Wesleyan's campus," she said. "I loved how it gave the town a sense of community and I think that effect has only gotten better over the years."

Smith said downtown Delaware is going in the right direction.

"Merchants know how to cater to individual taste in Delaware," she said. "It's because of this people see Delaware as an entertainment factor when they shop here."

Smith said the newer businesses downtown definitely cater to student taste.

"Obviously some of the older businesses don't give student patronage a whole lot of thought because they don't have a lot of student customers," she said. "However, the newer businesses are targeted right to you."

However, Director of Events Jesse Carter said Delaware is growing rapidly and, because of that, students are not as vital to businesses as they used to be. "We have not seen significant renovation work and the major influx of new businesses solely because of OWU," he said. "But OWU is a significant factor. There are some businesses who still cater and rely heavily upon students and probably always will."

In August 2004, the city initiated a survey of downtown properties to capture current business growth and residential unit increase. The project summary commenced in January 2005. The survey results stated downtown Delaware has been undergoing a slow but consistent revitalization over the past 10 years.

Sandusky Street

In the past seven years about 46 buildings have undergone rehabilitation, said Christine Palmer, housing and neighborhood planner, and both public and private sectors have made significant investments.

Community Affairs Coordinator Lee Yoakum said downtown Delaware and OWU are more inter-related than people think.

"Without OWU, the city of Delaware would be without important educational, cultural, social and athletic outlets," he said. "Without the city of Delaware, OWU would lack the solid midwestern character that has been at its heart for more than 160 years."

articles.headline: Clinics, Games and Free Food to Highlight Community Day
articles.author: Mary Beth Scherer
articles.body:
The campus and local communities will be able to come together on Saturday and Sunday and celebrate community weekend. Both days are full of events and activities the entire community can enjoy.

"The goal of Community Day is to build bridges between the Delaware city community and the OWU community," said Emma Bricker, Community Day organizer. "Basically we are all one, and we need to learn more about each other."

Saturday will begin with the Second Annual President's Fun Run and Walk for Education at 8 a.m. The run will be followed by the Kids Battle of the Bishop Run. The Bishop run is open to kids 12 and under, Bricker said, and will give kids an opportunity to race against the Bishop.

The top 15 men and women in the fun run will receive prizes. The top 3 men and the top 3 women walkers will also receive prizes. Prizes include running gear, gift certificates to area restaurants and OWU gear, Bricker said. A post-race party is being provided by Chartwells at Selby Stadium.

At 10:30 a.m. restaurants in the area will provide a sampling of different dishes. Two of the familiar restaurants included in this sampling are The Brown Jug and Rudy Z's. The Alarms will perform as well.

At 11 a.m. a boys and girls lacrosse clinic will take place. The men's lacrosse game against Washington & Jefferson will follow at 1 p.m. The clinic and admission to the game are free.

On Sunday, there will be free admission to the baseball game vs. Wooster at noon. Gulla's Hot Dogs will provide hot dogs for $1.50 each. After the game, a free baseball clinic will be held.

Bricker said she encourages people to attend the events this weekend.

"We have so much to offer in town and on campus," Bricker said. "I'm a believer in jumping in with both feet. Come out and enjoy the community."

Stanya Doty of Baskets Unique is also helping out with the activities this weekend. She said she is glad to see the communities working together.

"I think its important that both parties support each other," Doty said. "I grew up in Delaware and Wesleyan has been a stranger to me. When both groups get involved, they have a lot to offer each other."

Doty said she looks forward to getting her kids involved and would like to see the local people come out for the festivities.

"Locals new to events will gain a lot from participating," Doty said. "Wesleyan is like a hidden gem, and the more OWU can show what they have to offer the better."

articles.headline: Computer Thief Or Robin Hood?
articles.author: Lars Sorenson '06
articles.body:
Dear Editor,

I have already written on this topic before, so I will try to be brief. (If Jerome yawns again, I apologize. I have not yet plumbed the depths of life's trivialities to a point where I could write a weekly column about them. I have much to learn in the art of unsolicited scribbling, and my name does not rhyme with "home" like his. Some guys have all the luck!)

The cover of last week's Transcript detailed the theft of two computers from Welch's computer lab, which occurred at some point over Spring break. While this is doubtless regrettable, it is important that we not draw the wrong conclusions from it.

In the past year, we have seen the closing of the 24-hour computer labs in Smith and Stuyvesant, the addition of the 24-hour lab in the library for fall semester and then the closing of this same lab for the present semester. That makes three 24-hour labs we have lost in the past year alone. Computers and computer labs are disappearing from OWU at a frightening pace. Clearly, the theft of two computers over Spring break is not an isolated incident.

I would like to formally ask Jason Ramsey, chair of WCSA's Technology Committee, and Tom Green, associate director of libraries, where are all of our computer labs (specifically 24-hour labs) going, what exactly do you do with all the computers from the labs you close, and what do you plan to do with the computers that are left to us now?

In the article published April 13, I read: "With the stolen computers, maintenance and security issues and Beeghly Library's computer facilities expansion, LIS (Libraries and Information Systems) may consider closing down more computer labs on the residential side of campus." This is followed by: "Before the burglary, Welch was going to be the only lab left open, but now that may be in jeopardy, Ramsey said."

Forgive me, but I'm confused. If Welch was to be the only lab left open, then no one was "considering" closing down more computer labs; rather, it had already been decided that more computer labs would be closed. So which one is it? Are you considering closing more labs, or have you already decided? OWU students have a right to know.

The arguments one hears in favor of closing our computer labs boggle the mind. Tom Green says, "The closing of more residential hall computer labs (in Stuy and Smith) was part of the negotiations with WCSA that led to the 24-hour library space." This is quite the deal that WCSA made with LIS, then, considering that the 24-hour library space is no more. Can you imagine the negotiations?- "We'll give you two computer labs, but only if you promise to take one more at the end of next semester."

And chew on this: "Green said LIS decided to close the labs because of maintenance issues and they had received numerous complaints over the last few years about computers not working properly." So there are complaints about computers not working properly. Alright, what should we do about it? Clearly, we have no choice but to get rid of the computers.

But this one takes the cake: "Green also said Ohio Wesleyan is an exception when it comes to offering computer labs in dorms, since most universities don't offer any."

I am blushing with shame as I write. The barbarism of it is unspeakable.

All that said, if any other computers turn up missing in the future, we'll at least know there is a chance they'll be put to good use, so long as WCSA or LIS don't get their hands on them. (As consolation, you'll always have Jerome in your home. He's safe. Every university has one of these.)

Sincerely,

Lars Sorenson '06

articles.headline: Tigers have no answers for Bishops
articles.author: Phil Salisbury
articles.body:
Led by sophomores Chris Eccles and Steve Fowler, the Bishops scored 11 consecutive goals in their victory over Wittenberg 13-6 yesterday at Selby Stadium.

The game was tied 2-2 at the end of the first quarter when Ohio Wesleyan (7-4, 4-1 NCAC) took over, scoring the next 7 goals and never leading by less than 5 afterwards.

Coach Sean Ryan said he thought the team played outstandingly in the second quarter.

"We were flying all over the field and dominating play," Ryan said. "We need to continue that style of play for a full game. The second quarter was OWU lacrosse."

Fowler scored with 13:49 left in the second quarter, followed by a goal 45 seconds later by freshman Phillip Johnson to give the Bishops a 4-2 lead.

Ryan said Eccles, who has tallied 11 goals and 5 assists in the past two games, is playing how he wants all his players to play.

"Chris is a quiet kid that gives 100 percent all the time," Ryan said. "I think his actions are what make him a good leader."

Ryan said he likes the way the team played, but, at the same time, there is still room for improvement.

"The defense is playing well," he said. "They were able to swarm on double teams. The offense is clicking. The fact that they scored 4 goals in transition is my concern that we need work on."

Eccles scored three consecutive goals to close out the first half and give OWU a 9-2 halftime lead.

During the second half, tensions between the teams escalated almost to the point of a fight between the teams.

"Emotions run high in a game," Ryan said. "That was the only way I felt that they affected our overall play. It seemed to affect us more in a negative way. We need to get ready to play the next play and not dwell on what just occurred."

Eccles led the team with 6 goals and 3 assists, Fowler scored 3 goals, and freshman Eric Turner contributed 3 assists.

Sophomore Ryan Perrone had 9 saves in goal.

In other NCAC action, Eccles scored with :01 left in the first overtime to give the Bishops a 14-13 win over Wooster.

Freshman Karl Zimmerman scored to tie the game late in the fourth quarter.

Perrone had 9 saves in goal.

articles.headline: Duke's lacrosse team taints athletes
articles.author: Adam Guy
articles.body:
the victim.

Two players, Reade Seligmann and Collin Finnerty, were indicted Tuesday and charged with first-degree rape, sexual offense and kidnapping. They were released on $400,000 bail each. District Attorney Michael Nifong said a third player will likely be indicted.

According to the New York Times, on Thursday March 23 when Nifong said he was "convinced that a rape did occur," most of his beliefs rested on evidence gathered and he originally relied heavily on the DNA evidence. The DNA evidence, however, came back negative on Wednesday April 11.

According to the Herald Sun, another local paper, a candlelight vigil was held on Saturday March 25 to protest the crimes and called for the lacrosse players to speak out about the incident.

Reportedly the team is refusing to talk to investigators or anyone else about the incident. Protesters have even printed pictures of the lacrosse players and passed them around campus in hopes that the players will come forward.

According to Duke News, the school paper, the team captains issued a statement on Tuesday where they admitted to throwing a party, hiring dancers, and providing alcohol to minors, but they also said, "We also stated unequivocally that any allegation that a sexual assault or rape occurred is totally and transparently false."

The captains also stated that they feel they should not play competitively until the matter is resolved.

President Richard Brodhead has suspended the lacrosse team's season indefinitely and all games that are not played will be considered a "No contest" which will not affect their record.

The events of the past month at Duke have stirred up a frenzy of controversy. But have people jumped to conclusions to quickly?

Are the accounts of the women accurate and has the District Attorney counted all his eggs before they have hatched?

The woman worked for an escort service, and according to the News and Observer, had been on several "private dates" before. Could she have used a previous rape and pinned it on the lacrosse team to get back at the team for their racist comments?

The District Attorney said in interviews that once the DNA evidence comes back, he will have all the proof he needs. But what if the evidence doesn't support his claims?

Regardless of the outcome, the team could still have the accusations looming over its head for years to come. One must think of the Kobe Bryant case. He was eventually acquitted of all charges, but before that, nearly everyone (minus Lakers fans) were convinced of his guilt because the media and protesters made such a big deal out of what was "alleged" and not of what was "concrete" evidence.

Student athletes need to realize what they are doing before they go and do it, and, if there is ever any doubt that what they are doing might be wrong, then it probably is wrong.

Lacrosse is one of the fastest growing sports in America, and on Tuesday, March 13, it was shoved into the national spotlight when the Duke men's lacrosse team was accused of raping and sodomizing a woman at a party thrown at the house of the team captains.

According to the News and Observer (Durham N.C.), two black exotic dancers were called to a house where they believed they would be dancing for a small bachelor party. When they arrived, there were reportedly thirty or so lacrosse players awaiting the show.

A neighbor claimed the women left the house shortly after arriving while the men inside yelled racial slurs such as "Tell your grandpa I said thanks for the cotton shirt!" and "I want my money back!" Then a man came out of the house and convinced the women to come back into the house.

It was then that one of the women was allegedly pulled into a bathroom and raped by three males, who were apparently all lacrosse players and all white.

The Duke lacrosse team should not be in this situation in the first place. They are a nationally-ranked program respected throughout the country.

Any coach will tell you that a college-level team is not just a team, but an ambassador to the school; people look up to and respect them. By throwing this party and hiring dancers, they automatically put themselves in a situation that had the potential to harm their reputation and their season.

articles.headline: DiTraglia credits hard work
articles.author: Ted Thode
articles.body:
Senior Nina DiTraglia is a talented runner who has really grown as a runner in the past four years on the women's track and field team said Coach Kris Boey

"She is an enjoyable person to coach," Boey said. "The season is not over, and I am missing her already. She embodies everything I want out of a person on the team.

Boey said she is big part of the women's track and field team.

"She leads by example," Boey said. "Obviously every team likes to have that."

DiTraglia said she tries to support every single girl on the team. She said team success is important to her.

"It's fun to win individually but it's more fun when the team wins."

Boey said DiTraglia has really progressed throughout her career.

"As a freshman, she was the MVP of the cross country team," Boey said. "Her sophomore year was a down year for her. Her junior year was a breakout year. She broke four school records. Three individual records and one relay record."

DiTraglia said her improvement as a runner is all due to her hard work.

"I followed the coach's training and show up every practice." DiTraglia said.

Boey said DiTraglia normally runs the 5,000 meter but recently she also ran in the 1,500 meter race.

"She runs middle distance events but she really is a distance runner," Boey said. "She has some range. She can step down mainly.

Senior Meggie Feran said DiTraglia is a modest person who adds a sense of calmness to the team.

"She will never admit that she is awesome [at running]," Feran said. "But that's a good thing because you don't want the leader of the team to be into themselves."

Feran said before DiTraglia the team struggled in the long distance races.

"In the past, we have haven't been able to score in the long distance because the NCAC is so competitive," Feran said. "Finally we have [DiTraglia] who can score points in the long distance."

Boey said he thinks DiTraglia will hit the provisional time for Nationals.

"Right now, she is two seconds off the provisional time," Boey said. "In a seventeen minute race it's very likely she can make up those two seconds."

However, DiTraglia said even if she hits the provisional time for nationals, it doesn't mean she will go.

"It all depends how the other girls in [NCAC] do," DiTraglia said.

DiTraglia said she would not be disappointed if she did not make it to nationals.

articles.headline: No mercy shown
articles.author: Phil Salisbury
articles.body:
Potent bats powered Ohio Wesleyan to a sweep over Wabash and clinched a home series for the first round in the NCAC tournament.

The Bishops clinched first place in the NCAC West and will host the second place finisher in the NCAC East division on April 29-30.

Coach Tom Durant said even with a playoff berth, the starters won't necessarily get less playing time.

"The players tell me who's going to play [with their effort]," Durant said. "I don't want to rest them because they need to keep the focus and continuity. The conference tournament is important. They need the reps and the competition instead of resting them."

The Bishops won 10-0 and 10-4 on Friday, and on Saturday took both games of the doubleheader by scores of 14-3 and 14-6.

In Friday's opening game, OWU jumped out to a 3-0 lead in the second inning, with a 2-run double by freshman John Maggard followed by Maggard scoring on a single by sophomore A.J. Dote.

Senior Michael Krieger pitched a complete game, three-hit shutout.

In the second game, Dote went 3-3, with 2 HRs and 6 RBIs to lead the Bishops to a 10-4 win.

Durant said Dote is one of several players whose strong work ethic has translated to on-the-field success.

"They're starting to realize the rewards of hard work," Durant said. "In baseball, you need to put faith in hard work because it's a game of failure. You can go hitless for four games in a row. Good players can see past that. That's what a lot of players are starting to realize."

After allowing a run in the top of the first, the Bishops responded with four runs in the bottom of the frame when senior Brandon Williams stole home and Dote hit a 2-run homer.

Sophomore Sean Speed pitched 6 innings, giving up 4 runs to get the win, and freshman Kevin Miller pitched a scoreless seventh.

Despite winning four games over the weekend, Durant said there are always areas to improve upon.

"The pitchers over the weekend only had their fastballs; none of the off-speed pitches were working," he said. "We'll need strong pitching performances as well as hitting performances in the conference tournament. There are always things to work on from the previous week."

On Saturday, Williams went 4-5, scored 4 runs and had 3 RBIs and senior Kyle Sherman went 4-4 with a HR, 2 runs scored and 5 RBIs to pace OWU to a 14-3 win.

Durant said he was pleased with the patience his team showed when hitting.

"They worked the counts, made the opposing pitchers work harder, and got pitches they wanted," Durant said. "That's the key to our success: our ability to have good at-bats in productive situations. Even against Rowan, who is one of the top programs in the country, we had opportunities."

Senior Adam Dunn went the distance, giving up 7 hits and 3 runs to get the win.

In the nightcap, senior Sammy Hall and junior Tom Bottichio each had 3 RBIs to lead OWU to the sweep.

The Bishops scored 7 runs in the bottom of the third. Dote singled and drove in Maggard to start the scoring. Bottichio and Hall each hit 2-run home runs in the inning. Botticio also homered in the fourth inning.

Sophomore Xander Jones pitched a complete game, giving up 6 runs and 6 hits while striking out 6 batters as well.

"Denison and Wabash, the teams we beat the past two weekends, are good teams," Durant said. "We have the talent in the dugout to beat the best teams in the country."

In other action, OWU beat Ohio Dominican 10-9 yesterday.

articles.headline: Search for greek adviser underway
articles.author: Paige Burton
articles.body:
Interviews began Tuesday, April 11 for the greek adviser position.

Within the next two weeks, three candidates will be evaluated in the hopes of filling the position by the end of this semester.

Debbie Lamp, director of Student Activities and the Hamilton-Williams Campus Center, has been serving as the interim since Chris Cortina, assistant director for Greek Life and lacrosse coach, left last year.

Dean of Students John Delaney said that Lamp is a very capable person to have helping with the program, but that she is more than ready to hand off the day-to-day responsibilities of the position when a new adviser is selected.

Senior Justin McCoy, president of the Interfraternity Council (IFC), said the main duties of the adviser are to offer ideas on improving the current system and being knowledgeable about greek life.

"This person will have to be indispensable to myself," McCoy said. "So in other words, they are basically responsible for everything."

Panhellenic Council (Panhel) President Amanda Matthews, senior, said the primary role of an adviser is to assist with the paperwork and activities of running the Panhel, IFC and the National Pan-Hellenic Council (NPHC).

"While we currently do not have an NPHC on our campus, we do have a Panhel and IFC that are committed to developing strong greek life at OWU," Matthews said. "A greek adviser that advocates for the greeks and works to help them achieve their goals is necessary for this to happen."

McCoy said it's important to have a full-time person whose primary concern will be greek life.

"It's not that Deb does not want the job, so to speak," McCoy said. "[But] she has enough responsibility as it is, so implementing a proposed fall recruitment system and other student initiatives would be difficult."

Matthews said that Lamp simply does not have enough hours in the day to fill both positions since both require full-time attention.

McCoy said that the pay for vacant positions is typically not competitive, which leads to some of the vacancies not being filled as quickly.

Delaney said OWU is in the low-to mid-range of salaries for professional positions. The greek adviser position appears to fall into this category.

Another possible drawback for the job hunters could be the living situation, which requires the adviser to live on campus.

However, Matthews said she is not worried about the rule. She said such a requirement is not unusual for positions like this one.

"In some instances, greek advisers actually live in a fraternity or sorority house," Matthews said. "This situation is not so uncommon.

McCoy said a problem is only possible for a person with a family.

"If I were a former college student just starting a new life, the job might not seem that bad," McCoy said.

Delaney said he is excited about the prospective applicants.

"We have some strong candidates and it will be good to see how these folks match with the position and with our students, and how well we feel this will be a good fit for the candidates," Delaney said. "Student input and feedback will be a very important point of consideration in the selection process."

articles.headline: Phi Psi 500 helps Big Bros/Big Sisters
articles.author: Rachel Staff
articles.body:
Phi Kappa Psi's (Phi Psi) annual philanthropy event, Phi Psi 500, started Monday and will continue through the weekend, ending with a party on Saturday night at Topside Bar.

Phi Psi 500 is an annual week-long event to raise money for the fraternity's philanthropy, Big Brothers/Big Sisters. It is a competition between the sororities, with each event worth a certain amount of points.

Junior Brent Perrin, Phi Psi 500 chairman, said this event always raises a lot of money for Big Brother/Big Sister.

"This event is always a lot of fun for all the brothers and the sororities competing, and it's a great way to raise money in a fun way," Perrin said. "I especially enjoy Phi Psi 500 because it is a week-long event, not just one night."

Each sorority has to pay $60 to compete. On Monday the event kicked off, and each sorority hung their banner in Ham-Will. The one with the best banner promoting their "team" won points.

On Tuesday, each team had to pick a song and perform an air band skit at Vaqueros in front of Phi Psi and the other teams. The winner of this event also got a certain amount of points.

Tonight is Phi Psi's formal event and tomorrow the band Letter to the Editor will perform in Phi Psi's basement from 10 p.m.-12 a.m.

The main event is Race Day, which is Saturday at 1 p.m. The sorority teams can have as many members competing as they want, and Phi Psi has 4-5 people competing. It is an obstacle course and the winner adds points to their team's final score.

The week ends with a dance party Saturday night at Topside Bar (above The Strand) from 11:30 p.m.-2:30 a.m. for everyone.

Sophomore Phi Psi Tom Yaggi said this week is always a lot of fun for the brothers because it's a week of parties for them and everyone in the house gets really involved. He said it brings the brothers together at the end of the year.

"I really enjoy that all the brothers get to vote on which sorority wins each event and receives the greek points," Yaggi said. "I also liked how Tuesday night at Vaqueros isn't just the sororities performing skits, it is also to pay tribute to the seniors in Phi Psi."

Sophomore Alexa Deaton, a member of Delta Delta Delta, said she is excited for the upcoming events.

"I'm really excited for Race Day. It should be a blast, and this week is especially fun because it is the end of the year and it brings us all together before we leave."

articles.headline: Senior lunch a way for alumni to welcome grads
articles.author: Robert Louis-Charles
articles.body:
A 12-year Ohio Wesleyan tradition remains part of the graduating senior class celebration. The Annual Senior Class Luncheon will be held on Friday, April 28.

Alumni Relations Coordinator Brenda Dewitt said the goal this year is have 40 percent of the senior class attend the event.

"Last year, we were at 36 percent, but we think 40 percent is a good attendance figure, considering the number of students who have jobs or are student teaching during the day," Dewitt said.

The luncheon, she said, is the first alumni-sponsored event for graduating seniors. The Alumni Board uses this opportunity to welcome the graduating class into the Alumni Association.

"It also gives the seniors a chance to network with members of the Alumni Board; we try to keep things fun and casual," Dewitt said.

The planning for the luncheon started in January, Dewitt said, and with the assistance of Senior Class President Anita Chandrasekhar and Senior Vice President Dan Sharpe the outcome of the event will be successful.

Dewitt said the luncheon will include a brief program consisting of Dr. Nancy Morgan Giles '65, the chair of the Alumni Board of Directors; President Mark Huddleston; and Craig Luke '85, the chair of the Student/Alumni Relations Committee of the Alumni Board.

"The students will be asked to complete a survey followed by each senior receiving a gift from the Alumni Board," Dewitt said.

Dewitt said in her three years of planning this particular event there have not been many changes because the Alumni Board tries to keep the event casual and fun, while respecting the limited, available time of the students.

articles.headline: Historic Merrick, Vacant Since '80s, to Be Renovated
articles.author: Lainey Cullen
articles.body:
During the next year, Merrick Hall will undergo an exterior renovation which will open the door for the eventual complete renovation of the 19th century building.

George Elsbeck, vice president for Business Affairs, said the University has received two grants totaling $347,600 from the federal government to renovate Merrick's exterior facade.

"The grants represent two requests made by OWU in recognition of the needs of Merrick Hall," Elsbeck said. "The work planned for Merrick Hall is repair and replacement of the roof and cupolas, gutters, and downspouts and tuck pointing (repair) of the exterior."

Merrick Hall's cupolas, the ornamental structures on top of the roof, represent one of the building's unique design features. Gutters are the drains built along the eaves of the building to catch and channel rainwater to the building's downspouts, which are vertical pipes used to drain rainwater from the roof. Tuck pointing is patchwork of the mortar joints (cracks) between bricks or stones with a narrow ridge of putty.

Elsbeck said renovations of other buildings, including the Conrades Wetherell Science Center, Corns and fine arts facilities were deemed to be higher priorities than Merrick. Consequently, the University was forced to delay the renovation.

The Greek revival-style building is one of the 12 campus buildings on the National Register of Historic places, which makes it eligible for federal grants, according to the OWU web site. Elsbeck said renovation cost estimates from a few years ago were in the $5 million to $6 million range.

Elsbeck said the exterior renovation will begin, depending on seasonal weather conditions, when the full funding is in place. The University does not have the money to completely renovate Merrick Hall at this time.

In a Fall 2005 Transcript article, Elsbeck said the cost of renovating Merrick Hall exceeds the cost of tearing the building down and rebuilding it.

"Especially for older buildings, it may be less expensive to raze a building and then build a new," he said. "However this does not take into account the historic nature of older buildings."

Elsbeck said both grants have been authorized; however, the renovation is estimated at $450,000 and the grant funding totals $347,600. Elsbeck said the University has received other funds, including a gift from Richard Alexander '82, but the project still needs $50,000 before its commencement.

In a Fall 2005 Transcript article, Crosman said she believes Merrick Hall is likely to be one of the target projects for the University's next Capital Campaign, which is currently in the planning stages.

Elsbeck said the University will target interior work some time after completion of the exterior renovation. However, Elsbeck said he is currently unaware of the work that will be conducted within the building, predominantly because the University has not determined how Merrick will be used.

"Uses will be determined through a consultative process with faculty and staff as well as others" Elsbeck said.

Merrick Hall was completed in 1873 and housed the Alumni building and Science Hall, according to 100 Years of Excellence: A Pictorial View of OWU. The building provided quarters for Science Professor Edward T. Nelson, Chaplain L.D. McCabe and Mathematics Professor Hiram M. Perkins. The third floor, initially built as a chapel, housed a science museum.

The first greenhouse was attached to the south side of Merrick Hall during the 1890's, according to the Botany/Microbiology web site.

The building was constructed at a time when the University was forced to make important campus changes to allow for post Civil War enrollment increases and the installation of a new curriculum with a greater emphasis on science.

Merrick is named after Fredrick Merrick, second president of OWU from 1860-1873.

According to 100 Years of Excellence: A Pictorial View of OWU, Merrick worked as a "financial agent, professor, president, auditor, lecturer and trustee. He taught science, mostly chemistry, philosophy, law and other braches.

"Remarkably in his versatility, he stands out as a type of older general utility professor; mystical and saintly in disposition, he was at the same time a money-raiser," wrote author Barbara Mitchell Tull. "Less teacher or preacher than some of the other, he was unequalled in his solicitude for the spiritual and moral welfare of the students, in his zealous hard work for the college."

In 1962 the science department moved from Merrick Hall to the then newly developed and expanded facilities in Bigelow-Rice Hall. The second OWU greenhouse, named after Claude E. O'Neal, was attached to Bigelow-Rice.

In a Fall 2005 Transcript article, Karen Crosman, director of corporation and governmental relations, said Merrick Hall has been vacant since the late 1980s.

Chris Setzer, director of Building and Grounds, said, "outside of patching the roof," he has not done any work on Merrick Hall.

Setzer said the goal will be to maintain the original architectural style of Merrick Hall's exterior as close as possible.

"For example, the slate on the roof will be replaced with slate but an oil or latex paint will be used in lieu of lead paint," he said.

Setzer expects the exterior renovation to take 9 to 12 months. He said the current condition of Merrick Hall is unstable and the building needs to be renovated.

"B&G will be involved in the architectural and engineering design work for Merrick Hall," he said. "We will also issue and administer the construction contracts for the renovation."

Setzer said the project scope is larger than B&G can do because Merrick Hall requires a modern, technologically upgraded interior, including installation of all new plumbing, heating and electrical work.

Setzer said B&G will hire architects and engineers when it comes time to begin the renovation.

articles.headline: Student Documentaries Hit Strand
articles.author: Evan Ozimek-Maier
articles.body:
Celebrating its second year, the OWU Documentary Film Festival, which returns this Friday, has annually presented an eclectic mix of documentary shorts. This year's films, which were shot as honors projects for the Visual Anthropology course, are no different, showcasing the many sides of OWU and central Ohio. The films in this year's series are:

•OWU Haunts
•Old Man from the Mountain
.The Little Brown Jug

The festival begins Friday at 7 p.m. at The Strand Theatre, with a brief discussion after each film. Admission is free.

OWU Haunts

OWU is haunted. Well, so suggests OWU Haunts, a documentary by Anita Chandresakhar Erika Fox, Jody Vasileff, Jessica Walz, and Melissa Yinger. Chronicling both some of the many historical apparitional tales set on the Ohio Wesleyan campus as well as some more recent encounters, the film plays like a documentarian's campfire-side ghost story.

Ultimately, it is the film's use of storytelling that stands as its biggest strength. Unsurprisingly, public safety officer John Ciochetty makes an appearance, telling some of his famous ghost stories and conducting a technological ghost hunt. But more captivating are the obscure personal accounts of spiritual encounters, as told by members of Chi Phi and Phi Delta Theta fraternities.

But don't be fooled, as the film is anything but a ghost hunt on film. Still, whether you're a believer or just want to hear some creepy stories, OWU Haunts is sure to please.

Old Man from the Mountain

In his documentary, Old Man from the Mountain, filmmaker Austin Steinmetz, '05 tells the story of Rick Crooks, an Appalachian metalwork artist. Though blinded at an early age by an accidental shotgun discharge, Rick currently leads a full life. An avid outdoorsman, devoted father, and talented artist, Rick, many say, is making the best of his disability.

Rife with shots of Rick hard at work on his latest piece of scrap metal art as well as photos of his most cherished lawn-adorning creations (including horseshoe cacti and a dragon made of spades), the film has a personal inventory feel. Still, redemption comes through personal anecdotes from Rick himself as well as his friends and family, providing an intimate portrait of a simple, strong, respect-worthy person.

Though handicap-centric at times, the film tells the hopeful story of finding happiness through the pursuit of a dream. Audiences will surely find a heartening message, as much of Old Man from the Mountain seems to be about talent overcoming adversity.

The Little Brown Jug

Produced and directed by Elaine Chun and Matt Saracusa, The Little Brown Jug tells, not surprisingly, the story of The Little Brown Jug horse race. Using historical retrospectives from various locals and horseracing aficionados, the film becomes as much a cultural portrait as it does a history lesson.

The film finds its balance through interviews with both Brown Jug officials and race passionate locals. Though managers' stories and descriptions serve their purpose, it is ultimately remembrances given by Delaware natives that tell the true "story" of the Jug.

But beyond talking head segments, the film is most charming in its aesthetics. Often populated with the colorful and eclectic sights and sounds of the Little Brown Jug without accompanying dialogue, the film becomes an all-but-static glimpse at an American institution. This is one for race fans, historians and traditionalists alike.

articles.headline: The Cost of Friendship Is $20 Per Year
articles.author: Meghan Hensley
articles.body:
I always told myself that I would not get involved in chat rooms or message boards.

I also tell myself not to drink before noon. Unfortunately, I never listen.

On September 4, 2005, I dropped $20 on a membership to the Green Day Idiot Club. For the $20, I get a full 12 months access to exclusive pictures, video and audio, chances to win tickets to sold out concerts, autographed CDs and other merch, along with Q & As with the band members each month and of course the Idiot Club forum where I can talk to Green Day fans all over the globe.

For the first month I logged about 125 hours and on average the same, up until Christmas break, on the forum. In October two members of the club delivered a three foot tall birthday card to drummer Tré Cool at their last concert of the American Idiot Tour that was "signed" by each member on the forum. Apparently he liked it. Currently there is one being made for bassist Mike Dirnt.

Each day, since Christmas, I have been logging less and less time on the forum, but still spend about an hour a day catching up on what I've missed. I have made friends with about ten other members that I talk to on a regular basis, three of which live in England. I have logged a total of 17 days 10 hours and 59 minutes since September. Pretty good if you ask me considering one girl I talk to has logged 41 days 14 hours and 25 minutes since October.

The forum has become a touchy subject with my friends. I swear I'm not addicted, but what can you do, when people don't understand why you do what you do.

Oh well.

On the forum I have discussed just about everything, including kitchen sinks.

The Idiot Club is not the only message board/forum/club thing that I am a member of, there are three more, and each is slowly taking over what little soul I have left.

The other three include the bands Fall Out Boy, New Found Glory and celebrity Bam Margera. The latter I only joined to get access to the pictures that were posted by the members, honestly. The other two I joined legitimately. I am a fan, although I don't post very often.

The problem with message boards is that you get the entire fan base of the band or famous person, from the 9 year-old-just-found-this-band/person to the 43 year-old-been-a-fan-since-before-they-sold-out, which causes for some interesting conflict.

The usual conflict that arises is how the newer fan isn't a "true" fan since they don't know every little detail including shoe size usually brought up by an obsessed fan.

Regardless of who is a member, these boards make a great place to meet other fans and talk about anything and everything. I encourage everyone to try them out. Remember, drinking before noon is still not a good idea.
