articles.headline: Supreme Court's Grave Mistake
articles.author: Andrea Minich
articles.body:
Equating college students to high school students is something most people would never think about doing. Varying skill, maturity and experience levels are a few of the more noticeable differences.

However, the members of the Supreme Court have a different school of thought.

The Supreme Court's denial in February to hear Hosty v. Carter, a college newspaper censorship case, has limited free speech and unduly verified a lower court's ruling.

In June, the Seventh U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that public universities have the right to censor student-published newspapers. The Seventh Circuit Court has jurisdiction in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin.

The court's ruling stemmed from Hazelwood School District v. Kuhlmeier, a 1988 case which restricted the freedom of high school journalists by allowing high school officials to censor the paper.

Equating high school students to college students is a serious mistake one that could have disastrous effects in the United States in coming years.

"Simply put, a slippery slope has been created," wrote Darry Beckstrom in the Feb. 28 Badger Herald (University of Wisconsin-Madison).

The court has tried to justify its ruling by saying that if the newspaper is funded by its university, the university should be able to exert editorial control. Student presses can become immune to the censoring by having university officials sign a statement saying the paper is a public forum and content restriction is illegal.

Hosty v. Carter began in 2000 when The Innovator, the student newspaper at Governor's State University in Illinois, ran an article critical of University faculty. Patricia Carter, dean of student affairs and services, called the paper's printer and told them they were not to print the paper unless she had priorly reviewed it.

Encouraging this type of behavior with its ruling, the Seventh Circuit Court is restricting student journalists from applying classroom knowledge to the learning laboratory of the newsroom. The court is asking for secrets to be kept and is, essentially, creating an opportunity for universities to turn their student newspapers into public relation machines.

"If a college has the right to step in and censor its student paper...their [the students'] education will be neutered," reads the March 7 staff editorial in The Post, a student newspaper in Athens, Ohio. "Part of that hands-on education means learning to be responsible for what they print, and if university officials think the student press is committing libel, they should file a lawsuit. If they are simply upset by what they read in the paper, they should have no right to pull the plug on the student press like frazzled parents withholding an allowance."

The staff editorial from the Feb. 23 Oregon Daily Emerald, (University of Oregon) expressed a fear of improperly trained journalists.

"Raising a crop of journalists that don't know how to properly fill their roles is a disservice to the public- a disservice that could result in corruption flying under the radar of journalists who were taught not to criticize," the staff wrote.

The Hosty ruling seems to deny and undermine everything a university is and stands for. College is a place for the free flow of ideas and a time when students explore new ideas. A campus is the last place free speech should be censored.

While courts can and do look to past cases for guidance, precedent doesn't always provide the right answers.

The Seventh Circuit Court started its discussion of the Hosty case with "Hazelwood provides our starting point." One can only hope "Hosty provides our starting point," won't be the catch phrase of a court somewhere else.

articles.headline: An Epidemic Of Huge Proportions
articles.author: Jaclyn Chapple
articles.body:
Sixty-five percent of adult Americans are categorized as overweight or obese, according to the American Obesity Association (AOA). It is the second leading cause of preventable death in the U.S. (smoking is number one) and causes at least 300,000 deaths a year.

The AOA defined obesity as "a chronic disease involving environmental (social and cultural), genetic, physiologic, metabolic, behavioral and psychological components."

Weight has always been a huge issue in American culture since weight is something you can change to enhance your beauty, as opposed to freckles or height. Because of this, weight is one of the biggest stigmas and sources of ridicule in today's society.

This is not just a vanity issue. The AOA said obesity increases one's risk of developing conditions such as high blood pressure, diabetes (type 2), heart disease, stroke and cancer. A report published in The New England Journal of Medicine said the average American life expectancy is 77.6 years, but that obesity could potentially cut an individual's life expectancy by between five and 20 years.

AOA said the age groups where obesity is most prevalent is among men ages 65 to 74, and among women ages 55 to 64. This may be due to the loss of physical activity as people get older. And while working men and women still have lunch breaks, there is often not time to work out and burn off the lunch calories.

The New York Times said the national average for obesity in children ages 6-19 is about 16 percent. The New York Times said the amount of time children spend watching television is a better predictor of obesity than what they eat or how much physical activity they get. These facts are due to the advent of television as a babysitter. With more and more women working, there is less time to play with the kids and this often results in faster, less healthy meals. The New York Times also said sweetened drinks like soda are increasing the obesity problem among children.

The Journal of the American Dietetic Association stated a strong predictor of youths being at a healthy weight as having two parents who are of normal weight. If the children are taught properly about nutrition in the house, the kids and the parents are more likely to be at a healthy weight.

The New York Times said Mississippi is the nation's most obese state (Colorado is the least), and that southeastern states have a higher obesity rate than northern states. This is due to the kinds of food people eat. In the South, there is a strong tradition of fried food and soul food. In the North, people have much healthier food choices as part of their normal eating habits.

The Center for Rural Pennsylvania published a study in The New York Times that said 20 percent of students in rural school districts were considered obese, which is higher than the national average of 16 percent. This is due to the fact that in the country there is more need for strong individuals who can help on the farm. On the other hand, inner city children are also getting fat because fast food is less expensive as opposed to healthier, more expensive organic foods. MSNBC said researchers found obesity rates similar to rural America in the poorest urban neighborhoods. The obesity prevalence is higher for people with less education.

Some options for treatment include dietary therapy, physical activity, behavior therapy, drug therapy, combined therapy and surgery. The New York Times said one drug therapy up for federal review, Acomplia, helps control appetite by blocking the same brain receptors that stimulate the "munchies" in marijuana smokers.

The problem is that people have never been taught about healthy food choices and are stuck into the "disease" mentality, rather than trying to cut down portions, eating healthier and doing physical activities.

The Surgeon General said the perception of obesity at all ages must change to focus on health and not appearance. The problem is not just health education, but goes deeper into our society in which people drive rather than walk and eat 730 calorie Big Macs with cheese at McDonald's as part of a normal American lunch.

Luckily, some places have begun to tackle the obesity epidemic. New York City's health commissioner requested that city restaurants remove trans-fats from their menus, according to The New York Times. The Center for Science in the Public Interest filed a lawsuit to ban sales of sugary beverages in schools. And New York City has decided to serve one percent and skim milk in schools, according to The New York Times.

These are just a few steps toward dealing with an issue that is clogging our society.

articles.headline: A Generation Out Of Touch
articles.body:
In this fast paced, entertained society, it's no surprise that news programs like The Daily Show, Sportscenter, and Entertainment Tonight are the choice of college students for their news source.

Many of the usual news networks (NBC, ABC, CNN, FOX, etc.) are faced with competing against the unconventional news programs. The 18 to 22 demographic, raised on Nintendo, have ADD tendencies. We expect things to be entertaining and last only as long as our 5 second attention span allows us to focus on any one thing.

As a generation, we are quite apathetic about what is going on around us. About one in five as of 2002 read a newspaper, down from one out of every two in 1972. Even news sources publishing online has not drastically increased the numbers. Not only is news readership affected, national news programs are as well.

Many of us probably knew that Bucky Covington was voted off American Idol and that Katie Holmes and hubby Tom Cruise just announced the birth of their first child together. But did you know that six retired generals are demanding that Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfield resign? Or that earlier this week the United States deployed four warships to the Caribbean, right in Cuban President Fidel Castro's backyard, just in time for the 45th anniversary of the Bay of Pigs invasion?

The problem of low interest in the news could be a result of the overload of information available to us. At our age, our parents had a limited selection of where to get their news. Usually they had a choice of local radio stations and newspapers that ran national information along with the 3 major news networks (NBC, CBS and ABC), if they had television. Just at OWU, we have our choice of news networks including NBC, CBS, ABC, CNN, CSPAN, CSPAN-2, CNBC, MSNBC, BBC America, FOX News, plus ESPN and ESPN-2 for sports news and E!, MTV and MTV2 and VH1 for entertainment news. And that list doesn't even include the Internet options. But many choose to let apathy take over.

As adults we should know what is going on in our world, especially in our country. Take the time and at least read the headlines in a newspaper to get an idea of what is taking place outside of OWU. You know, that whole immigration debate would probably be a good thing to know something about.

articles.headline: Grades Don't Matter
articles.author: Ben Walkuski
articles.body:
I am often guilty of making mountains out of molehills. In fact, I have become quite skilled at turning something that may be nothing at all into the biggest deal ever. That's certainly a fault of mine. What I am not guilty of, however, is putting too much emphasis on grades. In fact, I am proud to say that I know exactly where letters such as A, B, C, D, and F belong: in the alphabet.

More than anything else in college life, I see and hear people make so much of grades. Some people feel obligated to keep up their grades in order to sustain their scholarship money; others want good grades so their parents will keep paying for their schooling; while others, still, just like the look of an A versus a B, or a B versus a C, and so forth.

As far as I'm concerned, grades don't matter. I know I am going out on quite a limb by saying that, but there's an important reason why I took such a risk: because I'm right.

Contrary to what may be a popular belief, employers tend not to care what your grades were in college. Instead, employers are far more concerned with something a little more relevant: whether or not you can get the job done. Beyond that, they are interested to a certain degree in who you are, how hard you will work, and how well you will work with others. All of these are relevant and appropriate things for an employer to know before hiring you. Are you going to let an A versus a B or a C, then, define who you are, how hard you will work and how well you will work with others? Are you going to build up those silly little letters to represent you? Individual, one-in-a-million, fabulous, precious, intelligent, you?

I would hope not.

Picture this: you work hard—I mean REALLY hard—all throughout high school, all throughout college, and graduate with a stellar grade point average. You are very proud of yourself—and at your first big job interview after college you cannot WAIT for your potential employer to find out how smart you are. Except here's the thing: you've interviewed for seven jobs and not once were you asked how you performed academically, what sorts of grades you got or even what your GPA was. Instead, you awkwardly answered all of the other questions they asked you... but secretly wished your head was buried in a book. After all, books were pretty much the only things you acquainted yourself with in college.

Oh, and by the way—you didn't get any of those jobs you applied for. You know why? Because you thought grades mattered. You thought that a little number, based on a bunch of little letters, meant the world.

Ask yourself: "What if no one ever asks?" In other words, what if no one ever asks you about your grades in college? What if no one cares? Will they still matter then?

My point, as my point so often is, is not to let other people drive you. Never allow what other people think, feel, or say to define who you are. Unless, of course, upon your death you'd like your epitaph to read as follows:

"Here lies (your name here). (S)he got A's."

articles.headline: My Campaign
articles.author: Jerome Stenger
articles.body:
Walking to class, I see a baby bird entangled in a neon flier. It must be election time at OWU! At the moment I'm trying to get an extension for my campaign since I applied after the deadline for senior class president and senior class representative. I still have a slim chance though.

The only way I can still win is if you are a Transcript editorial board member and you're reading this on Wednesday night. The voting has just taken place. Go to the WCSA room, wherever that might be, and steal all the ballots. This will not assure me a place on the candidate roster, but it sure will be a hassle for them. Leave a note stating, "Add Jerome to the roster or New Found Glory goes down, and also, Jerome didn't do this."

If this plan works, don't publish my campaign promises.

JEROME'S CAMPAIGN PROMISES

. I will find out what angus meat is and why it is taking over the country.

. I will make sure that anyone who complains about food on our campus is put to death in a grinder, which will ultimately produce next week's meat in the Bishop Café.

. I will see to it that the $40,000 trust fund that buys new garbage cans every year is used on something other than buying new trash cans.

. I will shop at Wal-Mart because, darn it, it's convenient.

. I will never wear a pink shirt, and if I drink too heavily one night and accidentally put one on the next morning, I will not pop its collar.

• I vow to take down any stray Frisbee thrower in my path, whether it's with a knife to the kidney on the JAYwalk or it's with a pellet gun from my second floor House of Thought window overlooking Welch Lawn.

• OWU bicycle rentals. This is my only real idea.

. I will bring back "chest hair."

. I will sentence death to any OWU Facebooker with the following profile pictures:
--someone who is not them
--them, holding a plastic cup
--them with their shirt off (guys) or showing an inappropriate amount of cleave (girls and guys).

. I will squelch the fad of students trying to lock British.

. I will burn all shirts that say "College" unless it's the one I wear.

• I will rip down all fliers of my competitors, and on my fliers, not list my selling points, but rather, make fun of the other competitors.

. I think a vibrating cell phone in class is more annoying than a ringing one.

. I will not use campaign fliers to show how "quirky" I am.

• I will sentence death upon anyone who chooses to engage in the "soda/pop" debate.

. I will frame any person for $10

. I will punch them in the neck for free.

articles.headline: Horoscopes
articles.author: Nicole Mills
articles.body:
Aries (March 21 to April 20)
On your walk to class, you will throw caution into the wind and jump into the pit of "LAVA" in front of the Creative Arts House.

Taurus (April 21 to May 21)
Instead of writing those last few papers, you will take to throwing cheese cubes out of your dorm window onto the 4 p.m. sun-bathers.

Gemini (May 22 to June 21)
After your professor has enumerated MANY times that the final will NOT be cumulative, a fellow classmate will approach you at lunch and ask if the final is going to be cumulative. Unable to control yourself, you will say "Yes. In fact, I think she mentioned that we will be tested over what she taught last semester as well. I hear it's going to be impossible."

Cancer (June 22 to July 22)
Tired of dodging the noontime Frisbee guys on the JAYwalk, you will skip your 11 a.m. class so you can properly position yourself and your paintball gun. You'll show those disc-lovers who's boss.

Leo (July 23 to August 22)
You will be standing in line at the Library Café and hear the person in front of you order a Caramel ¡lazelnut Creamice. When your turn comes you will order one as well. When the first one is ready (i.e. the one that is NOT your's), you will sprint to the counter, grab the cup and jet out of there like none other. Ha. You showed them.

Virgo (August 23 to September 22)
You will be shocked at how different and beautiful The Transcript looks this week. You will send an e-mail to owunews@owu.edu to express your gratitude and love for the newspaper staff.

Libra (September 23 to October 22)
You will be seen constantly hovering around lunch tables and trash cans making desperate lunges at any left-over foods as your food points have dwindled to single digits.

Scorpio (October 23 to November 22)
After a little too much fun at 'Stretch on a Monday night, you will accept a bet to drink a full cup of water from the Sulfur Springs. Um, yeah...good luck with that one.

Sagittarius (November 23 to December 21)
You will not cease your battle with ResLife for off-campus housing next year. And you should not back down because that ninth phone call from your mother will do the trick. Keep at it, kid.

Capricorn (December 22 to January 20)
In a moment of infrequent wildness, you will disregard the prestigious internship you were offered for the summer to go penguin-watching in the Antarctic with your second-cousin.

Aquarius (January 21 to February 19)
As the year draws to an end, you still will not quite grasp the concept of entering Ham-Will on the right while people exit on your left. The glares people will continue to give you will continue to not phase you.

articles.headline: News Briefs
articles.body:
Today

Grace Poore '84 will present "Business Plan of An Artivist" at 3:10 p.m. in Corns 312

Anita Cochran will present "Searching for Planets Around Other Stars" at 4:10 p.m. in room 163 of the science center as part of the Science Lecture Series.

Saturday

The women's gender studies program will host "Girls Under the Hood" at 1 p.m. The event, held in the parking lot behind Beeghly Library, will provide hands-on learning about basic car maintenance. Refreshments provided.

The Creative Arts House will sponsor a yard sale from 1 p.m. to 4 p.m. outside its house.

A 5K Fun Run and Walk will start at 8 a.m. from Selby Stadium. Registration is $10 for students and $20 for everyone else.

Community Day will begin at 10:30 a.m. with free food from area restaurants at Selby Stadium. A free lacrosse clinic and game will follow the tasting.

Doors open for Springfest, featuring New Found Glory and Brandtson, at 7 p.m. The concert will begin at 8 p.m. Tickets are on sale through Friday for $10 (for students). Tickets at the door are $15.

Sunday

Community Day will continue with a free baseball clinic and a game vs. Wooster will start at noon. Gulla's Hot Dogs will sell dogs for $1.50.

articles.headline: Arts Briefs
articles.body:

Student Recital The department of music will present a Percussion Ensemble performance. Jemison Auditorium, Sanborn Hall, 3:15 p.m. The event is free and open to the public.

Documentary Screening Grace Moore ('84) presents a screening of her documentary on sexual abuse, The Children We Sacrifice. The Strand Theatre, 7 p.m. The event is free and open to the public. A discussion of the film will follow the screening.

SATURDAY

Senior Art Show Students of the department of fine arts will showcase their art work. Ross Art Museum, 6 p.m. The event is free and open to the public.

SUNDAY

Spring Concert The department of music will present a Spring Choral Concert, directed by Jason Hiester. Gray Chapel, 3:15 p.m. The event is free and open to the public.

TUESDAY

Orchestral Concert The department of music will present a performance by the Ohio Wesleyan Chamber Orchestra. The event is directed by Kenichiro Matsuda. Gray Chapel, 8 p.m. The event is free and open to the public.

Film Series The OWU Community Film Series continues with a screening of director Ming-liang Tsai's 2001 film What Time is it There? Tickets are $5.50 at the door. The Strand Theatre, 9:30 p.m. There will be an encore screening Wednesday at 7 p.m. with a discussion at the Mean Bean following the film.
